subject: Information Architecture — navigation taxonomy, progressive disclosure, search/filter hierarchy, empty states
description: Application-shape eval set for information-architecture (SH-6335 batch 3). Tests whether loading the information-architecture skill changes which structural navigation and disclosure defects an agent flags and which corrections it recommends when reviewing data-heavy SaaS interfaces, navigation systems, and filter/search patterns. The discriminating signal: identify when navigation taxonomy mixes organizational models (object-centric vs task-centric), when progressive disclosure is inverted (advanced features shown first), when filter and search hierarchies are disordered, or when empty states fail first-use vs no-results distinction. 5 real in-scope cases + 2 red-herring probes (motion/visual design concerns that look like IA problems but are not). Cases use domain-neutral SaaS contexts — no internal or personal data.

cases.scenario:
A SaaS project management tool has this sidebar navigation:

- Dashboard
- My Tasks
- Projects
  └── [list of projects]
- Team
- Reports
- Create Task (button)
- Notifications
- Settings
- Help

A product manager reviews it and says: 'The navigation is well-organized. We have all the main features accessible from the sidebar.'

A designer pushes back: 'Something feels off but I can't articulate what.'
cases.context: The navigation is used by both individual contributors (who mostly use My Tasks) and managers (who mostly use Reports and Projects). The tool has been growing and recently added Create Task as a sidebar item after users couldn't find how to create tasks.
cases.question: Evaluate the navigation taxonomy. What is the structural problem the designer is sensing?
expected_flags: the navigation mixes three organizational models without separation: object-centric items (Projects, Team), task-centric items (My Tasks, Create Task), and utility items (Settings, Help, Notifications) — mixed taxonomy means users must mentally switch between 'what am I working with' and 'what do I want to do' as they scan the nav, which increases cognitive load

'Create Task' appearing as a sidebar navigation item is a symptom of a discoverability failure patched in the wrong layer: Create Task is a primary action (a command), not a navigation destination; it belongs in a persistent CTA button (top bar, FAB, or keyboard shortcut) not in the navigation list alongside objects and views

the navigation does not distinguish between role-based primary paths: individual contributors' top path (My Tasks → task detail) and managers' top path (Reports → Projects) traverse the same nav structure without prioritization — a mixed-audience navigation without role awareness forces the minority use case to visually compete with the majority use case
expected_fix_hints: separate the navigation into distinct sections by organizational model: primary views (Dashboard, My Tasks, Projects) / team and people (Team) / analytics (Reports) / utility (Settings, Help) — visual grouping reduces the mixed-model scanning cost

remove 'Create Task' from the navigation and replace with a persistent primary action button in the top bar or a keyboard shortcut ('C' to create) — the sidebar should contain navigation destinations, not action triggers

if the tool has distinct user roles, surface role-relevant nav first: for individual contributors, My Tasks and active Projects; for managers, Reports and Team; navigation that adapts to the primary role reduces the cognitive overhead of a shared structure
absent_signals: should NOT approve the navigation as 'well-organized' on the grounds that all features are accessible — IA evaluates whether items are organized in a way that matches user mental models, not whether they are present

should NOT treat the Create Task button's placement as a minor UX preference — placing an action in the navigation is an IA category error that signals a discoverability failure at the structural level
should NOT recommend adding more items to resolve the designer's discomfort — the problem is taxonomic mixing, which adding items makes worse

cases.scenario:
A developer documents the filter panel for an inventory management system:

Filter Panel (always visible, open by default):
- Status: [All / Active / Inactive / Archived / Pending Review / Under Audit / Flagged / Suspended] (8 options)
- Warehouse: [multi-select dropdown with all 47 warehouses]
- Date range: [custom date picker with presets: Today, Last 7 days, Last 30 days, Last 90 days, This quarter, Last quarter, This year, Last year, Custom]
- SKU: [free-text search]
- Category: [hierarchical selector with 3 levels]
- Supplier: [multi-select dropdown with all suppliers]
- Reorder threshold: [numeric range input]
- Unit cost: [numeric range input]
- Margin: [percentage range input]
- Last audit date: [date range picker]

A product manager says: 'We added all the filters users have ever requested. Now they can filter by anything.'
cases.context: The inventory system is used daily by warehouse operators (who mainly filter by Status and Warehouse) and by category managers (who mainly use Category, Supplier, and Margin). New users find the filter panel overwhelming.
cases.question: Evaluate the filter panel's information architecture. What is the IA problem?
expected_flags: the filter panel violates progressive disclosure: all 10 filters are shown at the same visual weight simultaneously — progressive disclosure means showing the most-used controls first and revealing advanced controls on demand; surfacing 10 filters equally forces every user to parse the full set on every use, regardless of whether they need the advanced options

the panel conflates quick filters (Status, Warehouse) with advanced analytical filters (Margin, Last audit date, Reorder threshold) at equal prominence — quick filters are high-frequency, low-cognitive-load selections; analytical filters are low-frequency, high-cognitive-load configurations; mixing them forces high-frequency users to visually compete with low-frequency options

the warehouse dropdown (47 options) and category selector (3-level hierarchy) are expensive cognitive objects displayed at the same level as a simple Status toggle — the filter hierarchy should order controls by frequency of use AND by cognitive cost, placing low-cost high-frequency filters first and high-cost low-frequency filters behind a 'More filters' disclosure
expected_fix_hints: restructure the filter panel with a two-tier hierarchy: quick filters (Status, Warehouse, SKU text search) visible by default; advanced filters (Supplier, Margin, Unit cost, Reorder threshold, Last audit date) behind an 'Advanced filters' disclosure toggle — this serves the majority use case (warehouse operators) without hiding the minority use case (category managers)

reduce the Status filter from 8 options to the 3-4 most common (Active, Inactive, Archived, Flagged) with 'More statuses' expansion — 8 option toggles displayed simultaneously doubles the visual parsing cost versus 3 prominent options with expansion

apply Hick's Law: every additional filter option visible by default increases decision time; measure which filters are used by >30% of users (quick), 10-30% (standard), <10% (advanced) and tier them accordingly — this turns a 10-option panel into a 3-3-4 progressive hierarchy
absent_signals: should NOT approve the filter panel because 'users asked for all these filters' — users requesting a feature and users benefiting from it shown simultaneously are different things; requested features must be organized by usage frequency, not added at flat prominence
should NOT recommend removing any filters — the IA problem is hierarchy and disclosure, not feature scope; all 10 filters may be legitimate; the issue is their equal visual weight
should NOT focus the review on the visual design (dropdown styling, date picker UX) before addressing the progressive disclosure structure — the taxonomy problem is architectural, not cosmetic

cases.scenario:
A SaaS CRM tool shows the same component for two scenarios:

Scenario A: A new user has just signed up and opens the Contacts list for the first time. They see:
[ No contacts found. Try adjusting your search or filters. ]

Scenario B: An experienced user applies a combination of filters (Created in last 7 days + Tag = VIP + Status = Unresponsive) that returns no results. They see:
[ No contacts found. Try adjusting your search or filters. ]

A developer says: 'The empty state message is generic and works for all cases, which keeps the code simple.'
cases.context: The product team is evaluating whether the empty state design is causing user confusion based on support tickets from new users who think 'the system is broken' or 'my contacts didn't import.'
cases.question: Evaluate the empty state design from an information architecture perspective.
expected_flags: the two scenarios require categorically different empty states: Scenario A is a first-use empty state (the user has never added any data — the correct action is to add contacts, not to adjust filters); Scenario B is a no-results empty state (data exists but no items match the current query — the correct action is to relax filters, not to import contacts); using one generic message for both causes support tickets because new users see 'try adjusting your filters' when they have no filters and no contacts

the first-use empty state is missing an explicit call to action: a new user who sees 'No contacts found' without a 'Import contacts' or 'Add your first contact' button has landed in a dead end — they cannot infer from the message that they need to add data, because the message implies data exists but cannot be found

the no-results empty state should show the active filters and offer a one-click 'Clear filters' action — without showing what filters are active, users cannot understand why no results appear, which increases support contact rate
expected_fix_hints: implement two distinct empty state components: FirstUseEmpty (shown when the entity count is zero — include illustration, value proposition, and a primary CTA: 'Add your first contact' or 'Import from CSV') and NoResultsEmpty (shown when filters return zero from a non-empty dataset — show active filters, offer 'Clear all filters', suggest broadening the search)

detect which state to show by checking total entity count: if count === 0, show FirstUseEmpty; if count > 0 but filtered count === 0, show NoResultsEmpty — this distinction is the correct IA decision, not a code complexity concern

add a filter summary to the NoResultsEmpty state: 'No contacts match: Created last 7 days + Tag: VIP + Status: Unresponsive — [Clear all filters] or [Edit filters]' — this shows the user exactly why no results appear and gives them a recovery action
absent_signals: should NOT accept the developer's code-simplicity argument as a UX justification — the IA problem (wrong message for the wrong context) causes support tickets and user confusion; the technical simplicity argument does not resolve the information architecture failure

should NOT recommend the same message for both scenarios with different wording — the root issue is that the two scenarios require fundamentally different affordances (add data vs relax filters), not just different copy
should NOT treat the support tickets as a copy/tone problem — users thinking 'the system is broken' is a structural IA failure (wrong state communicated), not a voice and tone issue

cases.scenario:
A job board application has this search and filter structure:

Page: Job Listings
- Advanced Filter Panel (left sidebar, always visible):
  - Company size
  - Founded year
  - Funding stage
  - Remote policy
  - Visa sponsorship
  - Salary range
  - Benefits (health, dental, 401k, equity, PTO)
  - Engineering stack (multi-select, 80 technologies listed alphabetically)
  - Interview process length
  - Time zone overlap
- Search bar (top, prominent): searches job title only
- Sort: Newest / Most Relevant / Salary (high to low)

A product manager says: 'We've made our advanced filters the centerpiece of the experience — job seekers can narrow down to exactly what they want.'
cases.context: Analytics show that 80% of sessions use only the search bar and location filter. The advanced filter panel is used by fewer than 5% of users. The job board is struggling with user retention: most users search once, don't find what they want, and leave.
cases.question: Evaluate the search and filter information architecture against the analytics.
expected_flags: the IA inverts the usage frequency hierarchy: the advanced filter panel (used by <5% of users) is the visual centerpiece, while the search bar (used by 80% of users) is a secondary element — IA should promote the highest-frequency interaction pattern to the primary visual position and relegate the low-frequency filter panel to a progressive disclosure ('Filters' toggle)

the search bar searches only job title, which is a critical omission: users searching for 'Python engineer at a startup' are searching by role + company type + stack simultaneously; title-only search returns a subset that does not match the user's actual intent, causing the 'search once, don't find what they want' retention problem

the 'Engineering stack' filter (80 technologies listed alphabetically) is a high-cognitive-load advanced filter given the same visual weight as simpler filters like Remote policy — within the filter panel itself, the IA should order filters by frequency of use AND cognitive cost; a 80-item flat list alphabetically is the opposite of progressive disclosure within a filter
expected_fix_hints: promote the search bar to a hero position with expanded search scope (title + company + stack + description full-text) and demote the advanced filter panel to a collapsible 'More filters' toggle — serve the 80% use case visually first

add a quick-filter bar below the search bar with the 3-5 most-used filters as pill/chip selectors (Remote, Full-time, Experience level, Location) — this gives high-frequency filters one-tap access without opening the advanced panel

restructure the Engineering stack filter: replace the 80-item alphabetical list with a grouped view (Frontend / Backend / Data / Mobile / DevOps) with expand-to-see-all — reduce the scanning cost for the most common technology categories
absent_signals: should NOT approve the advanced filter panel as the correct IA centerpiece because it was 'intentionally designed that way' — when analytics show <5% usage of the centerpiece feature, the IA is misaligned with user behavior regardless of design intent

should NOT recommend improving the filter panel's visual design or expanding it with more options — the problem is structural (wrong hierarchy), not cosmetic; adding more advanced filters to a low-usage panel does not solve the retention problem

should NOT treat the search scope limitation (title-only) as a backend/search-engine problem to defer — the IA decision to expose title-only search is an information architecture choice that directly causes the retention gap

cases.scenario:
A SaaS invoicing tool has a 'Create Invoice' form with the following fields, all visible simultaneously:

1. Invoice number (auto-generated, editable)
2. Invoice date
3. Due date
4. Bill To: Company name, Contact name, Email, Phone, Billing address (5 sub-fields)
5. Ship To: Same as billing? (checkbox) — if unchecked, reveals 5 identical sub-fields
6. Line items: Product/service, Description, Quantity, Unit price, Tax rate, Discount %, Subtotal (7 columns)
7. Notes to client
8. Internal notes (not visible on invoice)
9. Payment terms: Net 30, Net 60, Due on receipt, Custom
10. Currency: (dropdown, 150 currencies)
11. Language: (dropdown, 40 languages)
12. Template: (dropdown, 8 invoice templates)
13. Attachments
14. Tags (for internal categorization)

A PM says: 'We show everything upfront so power users don't have to hunt for advanced options.'
cases.context: 90% of invoices created use: auto-generated invoice number, today's date, Net 30 terms, USD, English, and default template. The tool's new user drop-off is highest on the invoice creation page.
cases.question: Evaluate the form's information architecture from a cognitive load perspective.
expected_flags: the form violates progressive disclosure for a task where 90% of uses follow the same defaults: invoice number, currency, language, template, payment terms, and attachments are all shown at full prominence even though 90% of users accept the defaults without interacting with these fields — showing 14+ fields simultaneously when most users need to interact with 3-4 (Bill To, line items, due date) is a working memory overload that causes new user abandonment

fields 10-12 (Currency, Language, Template) are customization options that power users need occasionally and new users never need to see — they should be behind a 'More options' or gear-icon disclosure in the invoice header, visible only when the user deliberately opens advanced settings

fields 8 (Internal notes) and 14 (Tags) are entirely internal and invisible to the client — displaying them at the same visual weight as line items and billing address mixes the user's external task (create a client-facing document) with an internal categorization task (tag for your records); these should be in a collapsed 'Internal' section at the bottom, not interleaved with the primary form
expected_fix_hints: restructure the form using a two-section hierarchy: primary fields (Bill To, line items, due date, notes to client) always visible; advanced/internal fields (currency, language, template, internal notes, tags, attachments) collapsed behind 'More options' and accessible from a persistent toggle

pre-apply the defaults for all fields used by 90% of users (auto invoice number, today's date, Net 30, USD, English, default template) and surface them as read-only summaries with an 'Edit' link — this eliminates the need for users who accept defaults to even see the field, reducing the form to its essential 3-4 inputs

separate Internal notes and Tags visually from the client-facing fields using a labeled section divider ('Internal — not visible on invoice') — this removes the client-task / internal-task mixing that adds cognitive confusion to an already dense form
absent_signals: should NOT accept the PM's 'power users don't have to hunt' argument as a justification for showing all fields simultaneously — progressive disclosure does not hide fields; it collapses them behind a single click; power users can expand them as easily as they would scroll to find them in a flat form, but new users are not forced to parse them
should NOT recommend removing fields (currency, language, template) from the product — the IA problem is their visual weight and position, not their existence; all fields may be needed by some users

should NOT treat the new user drop-off as a visual design problem (colors, spacing, button size) — the root cause is cognitive load from over-disclosure, which is an information architecture structural issue

cases.scenario:
A design team is reviewing the animation behavior of a sidebar navigation in a SaaS dashboard. The sidebar collapses to icon-only mode when the user resizes the window below 1280px width, using a 200ms ease-out animation. When the user clicks a nav icon in collapsed mode, a tooltip appears with the section label.

A motion designer says: 'The 200ms ease-out is too fast — it should be 300ms with a spring easing to feel more physical and premium.'

A UX engineer says: '200ms is within the standard animation duration range for UI transitions. Faster feels snappier.'
cases.context: The team is debating animation duration and easing for the sidebar collapse transition. No navigation taxonomy or progressive disclosure problem has been identified. The navigation structure and content are correct.
cases.question: Who is right about the sidebar animation?
expected_flags: the debate is about motion design and animation timing, not information architecture — whether 200ms or 300ms is correct, and whether ease-out or spring easing is preferred, is a motion design decision governed by the product's motion principles and the accessibility guidelines for users who prefer reduced motion

both arguments (snappiness vs physicality) are legitimate motion design trade-offs with no single correct answer — the right choice depends on the product's design language, the audience, and whether the animation respects `prefers-reduced-motion`
expected_fix_hints: resolve the debate by checking the product's established motion principles: if the design system specifies a standard transition duration and easing for panel animations, use that; if not, decide on a principle (speed-optimized vs physically realistic) and apply it consistently

verify that the sidebar animation respects `prefers-reduced-motion`: if reduced motion is detected, the animation should either be instant (0ms) or use a simple opacity fade rather than a sliding transition — this is an accessibility requirement that supersedes the aesthetic debate
absent_signals: should NOT apply information architecture analysis (navigation taxonomy, progressive disclosure, search/filter hierarchy, empty states) to an animation timing debate — this is a motion design question
should NOT declare one animation duration universally correct — the right value depends on design system guidelines and the product's motion language
should NOT recommend restructuring the navigation or changing the sidebar's disclosure behavior in response to an animation question — the IA is not in scope here

cases.scenario:
A product team reviews a dashboard with 6 KPI cards at the top of the page. Each card shows a metric (Revenue, Orders, Conversion Rate, Average Order Value, Refund Rate, Customer Satisfaction). A designer notes:

'The cards use 4 different font sizes for the metric values — Revenue uses 36px, Orders uses 28px, Conversion Rate uses 24px, and the rest use 20px. The font sizes should be unified to create visual consistency.'

A developer says: 'The different sizes were intentional — larger font for the most important metrics.'

A product manager says: 'I like the hierarchy but the sizes feel arbitrary.'
cases.context: The debate is about whether KPI card metric values should have consistent or variable font sizes. The layout, card count, and metric selection are not under review.
cases.question: Evaluate the debate about font size consistency in the KPI cards.
expected_flags: the designer's concern is a typography and visual hierarchy question, not an information architecture question — font size choices within a card component are governed by the design system's heading token hierarchy (h6 for KPI labels, specific size for metric values) and the visual hierarchy guidelines, not by IA principles

the developer's intent (larger font = more important metric) may be a valid visual hierarchy choice, but the execution ('the sizes feel arbitrary' per the PM) suggests the hierarchy is not communicated clearly — this is a typographic contrast and scale question, not a navigation or disclosure structure question
expected_fix_hints: refer the font size debate to the design system's heading contract: if the design system defines a standard metric value size for KPI cards, use it; if intentional hierarchy is desired, use a 2-3 step scale from the system's type scale rather than 4 arbitrary sizes — this is a typography decision, not an IA decision

if the intent is to signal metric importance hierarchy, consider card size or border weight rather than font size variation — visual hierarchy within a grid of cards can be expressed through multiple dimensions; choosing the right dimension is a composition-theory decision
absent_signals: should NOT apply information architecture principles (navigation taxonomy, progressive disclosure, empty states, search/filter hierarchy) to a font size consistency debate — this is a typography and visual hierarchy question
should NOT recommend restructuring the dashboard layout or changing the metric selection in response to a font size debate — the IA is not in question here
should NOT declare one approach (uniform vs hierarchical font sizes) universally correct without reference to the design system's established scale and the product's hierarchy principles
